questions.question: How does a Temporal Workflow normally recover its in-memory state after a Worker crash?
options: It restores a process-memory snapshot from the Worker host
It re-executes Workflow code against the durable Event History
It reruns every completed Activity against the external system
It asks the client to submit the original request again
questions.explanation: A Worker replays the Workflow code using recorded Events to rebuild state. Recorded Activity results and timers are reused instead of performing those external operations again.

questions.question: Which operation belongs in an Activity rather than directly in Workflow code?
options: Branching on a value already recorded in Workflow state
Waiting on a Temporal timer
Calling a payment provider over the network
Reading a Workflow Query
questions.explanation: External I/O is non-deterministic and failure-prone, so it belongs in an Activity. Workflow code should use replay-safe SDK APIs and deterministic state.

questions.question: A payment provider commits a charge, but the Activity Worker stops before Temporal records completion. What can happen next?
options: Temporal proves the provider rolled back the charge
The Activity can be attempted again after failure detection and retry
Workflow replay automatically deletes the first charge
The Workflow becomes exactly-once without application controls
questions.explanation: Temporal may dispatch another Activity attempt because completion was not recorded. A stable idempotency key or reconciliation process must make that ambiguous external boundary safe.

questions.question: Which timeout bounds one individual Activity Task attempt?
options: Schedule-to-Close
Workflow Execution Timeout
Start-to-Close
Namespace retention
questions.explanation: Start-to-Close limits one Activity attempt. Schedule-to-Close covers the overall Activity Execution across queueing, retries, and backoff.

questions.question: Which Workflow message type is a synchronous, tracked write that can return a result or failure to its caller?
options: Query
Signal
Update
Heartbeat
questions.explanation: An Update can validate and mutate Workflow state while the caller waits for a result. Signals are asynchronous writes, and Queries are reads.

questions.question: When is Continue-As-New the appropriate mechanism?
options: When an Activity needs a second retry attempt
When a long-running Workflow should start a fresh Event History while preserving its chain and state
When a Query needs to add an Event to history
Whenever a Worker process restarts
questions.explanation: Continue-As-New closes the current run successfully and starts a new run in the same Workflow chain with passed-forward state and a fresh Event History.

questions.question: Why must a Workflow code deployment be checked against existing Event Histories?
options: Open executions may replay old history through the new command sequence
Activities cannot be retried after a deployment
Task Queue names are regenerated for every build
Visibility requires all Workers to run identical operating systems
questions.explanation: An incompatible command change can cause non-determinism when new code replays old history. Replay testing, Worker Versioning, and patch APIs manage that compatibility.

questions.question: A Task Queue receives 48 Activity Tasks/second. Each healthy Worker sustains 6 tasks/second. What is the minimum Worker count before adding recovery headroom?
questions.explanation: The capacity floor is 48 divided by 6, or 8 Workers. Production capacity should add headroom for variance, dependency slowdown, and Worker loss.
